Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Tetragrammaton" <vam...@usa.com> wrote in message news:52f0d87d.03020...@posting.google.com...

> by the v:tes rulebook (Object of the Game):

> Your goal is to accumulate the *most victory points* by destroying the
> influence held by rival Methuselahs.

I think the different possible readings of this sentence may be
part of why you thought you have to try to get all the VPs.

In English, getting the most victory points could mean getting as
many as you possibly can. But it could also mean getting more
than any other player (since if you have more than all the others,
you have "the most").

The latter interpretation is what determines whether you've won
the game, and it also leads you to the conclusion that if you
have more VPs than anyone else, you have achieved the goal - that
is, it implies that having 5 VPs is not necessarily better than
having 3.

In practice, having 5 does mean you've won by a larger margin.
But a "won game", as in baseball, football (both kinds), etc,
doesn't have to be worth more if it's won by a larger margin
(and in other sports, usually isn't, except possibly in some
tiebreaker stat).

Josh

Clarification:
Playing for 2 VPs in the hope that two other players will
get 1 VP each is not "playing to win" - it's just playing
for 2 VPs (which is not a win).
If, however, your activity is constructed so as to accomplish
the goal of effecting the required VP distribution (the
obvious example being with a mutli-oust vote like Anarchist
Uprising), then that's playing to win. Playing to accomplish
a 2-1-1-finish is different than simply playing for 2 VPs
in the hopes that 2 will somehow be sufficient.

Well, it's always up to the judge to evaluate and give a
judgement call if other players are complaining that someone
at their table isn't playing to win. That's pretty much
the job of the judge. :-)

> Don't you feel that if players should have to play
> (from the very beginning)
> for "accumulating the most Vps" intended as
> *the maximum total Vps currently available*
> instead of
> *the most Vps needed to win at the table*
> we had a less-prone-to-collusion tournament enviroment ?

I'm not LSJ, obviously, but my feeling is that interpreting
behavior and its intent with regard to gaining X number of
VPs is subjective and difficult enough that there would be
no practical benefit to saying "you have to try to get as
many VPs as you possibly can" as compared to "you have to
try to get enough VPs to win the game".

That is, since there are any number of courses of action
that *can* be intended to end in a player winning the game,
even if they don't look especially effective just at this
instant, it's usually very difficult to finding any clear
evidence of collusion or game-throwing unless the person
in question actually flat-out says that that's what they're
doing. And so it seems to me that it would be, in practice,
nearly impossible to distinguish someone "playing for 3 VPs"
from someone "playing for 5 VPs" even if a rule that you had
to play for 5 VPs did exist. Therefore I don't think much
of anything could be gained by instituting such a rule, when
the rule we already have already prohibits people from
giving up their own chances of *winning* the game in favor
of helping someone else win the game.

Here's a hypothetical situation at a 4 player table:
W > X > Y > Z

It has been a long game and time is running short. W has lots of pool
and has destroyed all of X's minions. X is sitting on their meager
pool waiting things out. Y is on the verge of ousting Z by stealth
bleed. Z is playing politics, has no bounce and will absolutely be
ousted by Y on their next turn.

W and Z make a deal. Z will use their last ounce of political strength
upstream to oust Y. X will get the VP and pool, but W has enough
bleeding minions that it will only take a couple of turns to finish X
off. In exchange, W will allow Z to withdraw from the game (after
quickly cycling cards via Fragment of the Book of Nod), taking 1 VP
from the table.

So, on Z's next turn, he passes a couple KRCs, ousting Y. X gets the
VP and pool. W then bleeds X heavily eventually ousting X. Then, even
though W is now in a superior position and CAN oust Z, he honors the
deal and allows Z to withdraw. The table ends with W getting the Table
Win with 2 VPs, X has 1 VP and Z has 1 VP.

Is this legal?

>Win with 2 VPs, X has 1 VP and Z has 1 VP.
>
>Is this legal?

"Honor" is not the right word - W is a weasel while Z is a quisling.

As to legality:

a) Such deals are not sanctioned by the rules. If time is short, then
players shouldn't be wasting it by discussing them. If W can propose
such things then why can't Y propose counter-deals? Where does this
process end? When the clock runs out?

b) We are asked to believe that the VP which Z represents is worth
something to Z but worth nothing to W. So far as winning the game is
concerned, it is clearly worth nothing in the scenario described.
But, if it is still worth something as a tournament tie-break or
rating boost, then W should be striving as hard for it as Z. And so W
should oust Z.

c) In practise, the main reason that W would allow Z to walk away with
a free VP is the implicit threat of what will happen in future games,
if he doesn't - there will be boycotts, reprisals and so forth. Such
out-of-game considerations are collusion - only available to players
who know each other and make deals regularly.

If you want to explore such issues in a purer form, I recommend the
Survivor CCG. The mechanics are simpler and so allow you focus purely
on the popularity contest - a sub-game in which it is bad to be good
and it's good to be weak. In the one tournament of this that I played
(for a $500 prize), the two final players were a guy and an 8 year old
girl. The girl appeared to have trouble understanding the basics
(like which way up to hold the cards) but had a solid alliance with
the guy and, between them, saw off many players who were ostensibly
good. I myself went out in the first round because I foolishly gave
the impression that I knew what I was doing. In the final showdown,
the little girl gave the guy a fright by pulling up level so that the
result was decided by a single card but, alas, it was the guy who
pocketed the $500. I don't know if he subsequently gave her or a
parents a cut.

Andrew

>Now, as to what one *will* do after they achieve the Game Win, and there

>I've just achieved a Game Win in round 3, and I've swept the past 2
>rounds, it probably doesn't help me to go for the remaining VPs, so why
>should I?

In a very large tournament, it would be possible to carry on needing the
VPs, if other people were managing 3 table sweeps.

However, this comes back down to the basic point of deals:

- deals are legal, by repeated ruling and Garfield's own writings (he
sought to limit the amount of useful interaction players could
have, and use carrots like the Edge and 6 pool oustings to
encourage counter to uber-diplomacy, but he did not seek to
neuter them - see the political aspects of the game)

- deals must be legal when they are made. That is, you must be playing
to win or, secondarily, to maximise VPs. (This is well
understood.)

- honouring a previously made deal *even if there are better things for
you to do NOW* is legal

This third point is the tricky one. Outside of a simple, one-shot deal
like Succubus Club ("Okay, you give me the Direct Intervention and I'll
give you this Dreams of the Sphinx"), all deals have the capacity to
bite back.

Were you to rigorously enforce "You must *ALWAYS* play for maximising
VPs and the table win", this would result in a situation like:

W X Y Z (from previous post)

Z offers the oust-Y and withdraw deal. W takes it. Y is ousted. W
ousts X.

W now has to play for maximising VPs and the table win. So he HAS to
double-cross on the deal.

However, in the situation where the deal was made, this would be
obvious, so Z could never make the deal in the first place.

As a result, any slightly complex or slightly long term deal would
involve an element where one player would have to double-cross the other
and maximise their VPs and chance of ousting their prey, etc.

So deals have to be legal when made.

>> Why does he
>> cheat like this?

Obvious answer: Because it's not cheating. No rules have been broken,
and repeated rulings have stated it's legal.

>>Because he expects that his investment of 1 VP now
>> will pay off with more than 1 VP in future games.
>
>If anyone honors that in the next game, it's considered *out of game
>considerations*, and hence illegal.

In the situation that he expects some return from it in future games,
yes, that would be collusion.

However, all players develop a reputation and including that reputation
in your considerations is allowed. "No, judge, I don't want to make
that deal because he's a dirty double crosser and he won't go through
with it" is a perfectly legal reason for taking or not taking a deal.

Z may go on to develop a reputation of: "Oh, he was that smart guy who
knew his way round the 'play to win' rules, and made sure he got a VP
too. I don't know if I could've managed it if he didn't oust Y." When
coming up to time, this may well also be noted by spectators.

In later rounds, or other tournaments, clever play and subtle, legal
manipulation of the finer points of the rules may come back to aid a
player.

However, in situations where cutting a reasonable deal exist, with
increased chances of receiving a game win and the other player having
very little chance at all of receiving one anyway (e.g. a stealth bleed
deck that's been all but destroyed by a combat deck, but has one, last
vampire to throw at them, and does so), there is no problem. Both player
cut a mutually beneficial deal - right?

In situations where a deal is made which is rubbish and clearly not in a
player's best interests ("Oh, uh, yeah, you do that and I'll oust
myself," says the player with 75 pool and about to roll the table), a
judge can intervene.

In situations where VPs are just *given away* for no good reason, call a
judge over. The judge can first establish that it isn't either of the
above. So we are dealing with a situation where no overt, legal deal has
been made.

Perhaps you have a table A-B-C-D-E. D and E were combat decks, and E
could have cut through A like a knife through butter. D goes forward
heavily onto D, almost dying in the process. (Combat+Combat = Foom) A
could oust D, but lets D oust E first. This could be regarded as a
"Thank you" for stopping E ousting A and would be pretty much legal.
(Unless there was something else odd going on.)

A judge - using their judgement - could determine that a covert deal has
been made, or pre-arranged. It is understood that a judge always has the
option of stepping outside the Judging Guidelines where extenuating
circumstances exist.

In that case the answer is: it's up to the judge's decision.
The judge, when given the facts of the case, makes a judgment.
[LSJ 20020219]
<http://groups.google.com/groups?selm=3D8A0163.E3938FAA%40white-wolf.com>

Please remember that these are only guidelines. If the judge
believes that the situation has significant, extenuating
circumstances, he or she is free to modify the penalty as
appropriate.
[Judging Guidelines]

If there were no reasonable explanation for the VPs being given away, it
would not be beyond the realms of possibility for a judge to suspect
collusion, out-of-game considerations and so on. (This can be especially
true in the third round, when you have a good idea of who'll make the
final and who giving your 'spare' VPs to might exclude.) Where a player
can offer no reasonable motivation for their actions, it is perfectly
okay for a judge to suspect something. Bear in mind that this is not a
court of law, the judge is always relying on judgement calls and
balancing issues. For instance, "If a judge believes that an infraction
was intentional, the penalty should be upgraded as appropriate (see
section 160)." *If a judge believes*, not *If a judge can prove beyond
all reasonable doubt*.

Were such to occur several times in a tournament with the same player,
tracking it on paper would be an option. They cannot offer any reason
for their actions that satisfies the Head Judge, and the Head Judge (and
any other judges) suspect foul play. Extenuating circumstances (it
happening several times) may convince the Judge to issue a written
warning because they believe something is *wrong*, which is communicated
with V:EKN.

Similarly, if this happened every time in the third round with this
player over several tournaments, a judge could suspect foul-play,
collusion and so on.

They use their judgement.

Where things seem wrong, the judge has to use their discretion. Even
without having sufficient reason to issue a penalty, the Archon (if used)
allows Tournament Notes to be entered. A tricky decision such as the
above could well be entered, with the judge's thoughts on it. If such
happens multiple times, it's likely to come to V:EKN's attention. If it
doesn't, shrug your shoulders and move on.

It's a game.

stop after someone achieves the winning number of VPs.

than dismissed as unimportant to determining the winner of the game.

Let's go back to logic a second...

There are only certain VP combinations that will yield Game Wins.

Four-player table: 4/0, 3/1, 2/1/1, 2.5/0.5

Five-player table: 5/0, 4/1, 3/2, 3/1/1, 2/1/1/1, 3.5/0.5,
2.5/0.5/0.5, 2.5/1/0.5

There may be others, but I think that's covered the possibilities.

It is IMPOSSIBLE for there to be three players remaining at the
instant a Game Win has been determined for ANY table without going to
time. Logically, with three players remaining, only 2 VPs have been
earned, at best by a single player. Any of the remaining three players
can "sweep" and earn the Game Win. (There has been quite a bit of
discussion about the "three player game" on this newsgroup in the past
and strategies for getting to that point and collapsing the table in
your favor.)

Once a Game Winner has been determined, they will logically have at
most one opponent left, or, time will have been called.

I played in a tournament final where a situation like this had
occurred. The Giovanni "responsible bleeder" chose the Gangrel Wall as
his predator. The Giovanni secured 3 VPs ousting 3 consecutive prey,
leaving himself and his original predator standing. The Gangrel Wall
was a slow-building deck and eventually decimated the Giovanni with
combat, but they still didn't win the tournament.

Granted, it would be possible for a player with 3 VPs to face off with
their friend as the final 2 players, but I think it should be VERY
obvious to a judge in most situations if the 3 VP player simply rolled
over and died after earning 18 extra pool during the course of the
game.

A relatively extreme case of table-splitting I could imagine would be
with a Rush/Wall deck preying on a "friendly" stealth bleed/politics
deck. The Rush/Wall could keep themselves alive, while Rushing in
sequence, minions of the S&B friend's prey. After securing 3 VPs and
the GW, the bleed/politics deck would suddenly fall over and die to
repeated Fame/torpor after "over-extending" themselves.

In fact, IIRC, this is similiar to the situation which caused all
sorts of controversy at the Euro Champs last year. At that point, the
trick for the judges is determining whether the player is actually
playing to win or just survive. This can be very difficult to judge
especially if someone has a lot of pressure on them.

Anyway, I just wanted to point out that once a table win has been
secured, the rest of the game is usually easy to figure out. It's the
strategies and tactics used DURING the game that a judge really needs
to watch to determine if there is any collusion occurring.

been determined, they shouldn't be treated as if they don't matter by
the "play to win" rule.

An additional "spurious" rule should be added because in a tournament
setting, winning the game is not the only thing that's scored; non-
winning VPs also count toward tournament standing. So it doesn't
make sense for the rules to say that, once a game winner has been
determined, the winner has no use for the rest of the VPs - they *do*
have a use for them.

> Whether certain deals are affected is not the point.
> The point is: why impose an additional (spurious) goal on the game?

The goal's not spurious.

Consider an imaginary Scrabble tournament. In this tournament, you
add up the points you scored in each round as a tiebreaker, although
your standing is primarily determined by how many rounds you won.
Now, even though the rules of Scrabble tell you that the winner of
the game is the person with the most points, and it doesn't matter
how many more than your opponent you finish with, in this tournament
you're better off the more points you win by.

In such a tournament, your primary goal is to win each game by
having more points than your opponent. But your secondary goal is
to score the most points possible, because even if you don't win,
your tiebreakers will be better if you have more points. So the
"win the game" goal is not the only legitimate goal in this
tournament... much like in VTES.

Josh

It depends.

In a non-tournament game, playing for fun can be the most important
part. If it stops being fun, turn in your decks for the night and start
on something different.

However, playing for second in friendly play can be useful.

First of all, honing a deck - either for tournament play or for more
friendly play - is very useful. It might be that your deck needs real
work for the end-game. It gets decked very quickly, it gets into real
trouble because it was solely transient. That sort of trouble. Knowing
about this in detail helps you fix it.

Additionally, even if not in a real tournament, some people keep
friendly tallies of how well they're doing. In such instances, you need
proper results really.

On top of that, other people may well want to play fully to the end,
even if you see it as a foregone conclusion.

way for you to get 2 VPs rather than 0 VPs, maybe you'd want to go for
it. so you try to squeeze a little extra out of the rules.

As a judge, that's crap you *really* don't need.

It was about VP splitting in general, as an *extension* of action

>>

>But, i repeat, can't see how if Vps deals are utterly mimized

Because people are people. Maybe your people are robots or something.
However, the people I see around me every day and at tournaments want to
win and play competitively.

If you have some woolly rule about "You must play to maximise VPs
always" then you will get into interminable arguments. "But if I don't
make this deal now, I won't get any VPs anyway. And what are you
telling me to do, backstab someone after I've made a deal? WTF?"

win alone. Chances are, both will die on their own. A little team work
and boom, mutual co-operation.

I get 0 VPs, maybe 1 VP before I die. You get 0 VPs because you're
coming up behind me and we're just going to mutually annihilate each
other. Or I get 3 VPs (TW) and you get 2 VPs.

That's mutual co-operation, with each player playing towards in-game
goals.

If you'd like to be the one to explain to players "No, sorry, that
previously perfectly legal tactic that helped you both out yesterday is
now illegal. Yeah, I know I'm having to tell you both now not to
maximise your VPs or your table win chances but, hey, we have some new
rules that say you don't have to play for a table-win anymore if people
don't like the deal you're making. Sux2bu." then be my guest.

waiting to happen.

>>>

Try reading the whole post, dear. Not moot at all.

If a player or judge has good reason to suspect collusion, it matters
not what the current state of VPs is.

>So, say, with 2 players left at the table,

>by A minions,

judge always has leeway to intervene.

no reasonable suggestion for their actions may convince a judge to pay
more attention later on, even if they don't feel inclined to rule
collusion here.

If there is no reasonable suspicion of collusion, they don't act.

>>> Yes, but it would not be better if the Judge knows that a specific
>>> rule clearly forbides to a "3 alredy-scored Vps" player from
>>> "giving away" the remaining 2 ?
>>

>>

> Vps-dealing, and that would be not a bad thing, imho.

No, players who were better at explaining why what they were doing was
legitimate play and not VP sharing would not be tied up at all. Players
who weren't quite so quick with their explanations would be left tied up
in knots. The gift of creative explanation is not one we all have.

This is the sort of crap a judge doesn't need. Having had to sit down
and give rulings on tables where all three remaining players (I recall a
table at Gencon 2 years ago with Matt Green, Rob Treasure and *I think*
Jon Cooper) are more than capable of making extremely convincing points
about their style of play, it can be *extremely* hard to separate what
is right in the context of the game, what is right in the context of
what the players are entitled to believe and what is clever play on
their part.

In the context of the game: Are they doing what's right in order to
maximise their chances of a game-win? Are they maximising their VPs if
not?

In the context of what the players are entitled to believe: I am a
stealth bleed deck. You are an intercept wall, with bruise and bleed
edges. I cannot bleed through you. So, we come to some deal. As a
judge coming over to verify the deal, I can see both players' hands,
ash-heaps, possibly their libraries, and so on. Assume that I'm playing
the stealth bleed deck. Well, I can see that he's blocked or bounced
everything I've done so far, but he's not getting on so well with this
bleeds. However, if I then look at the intercept player, I can see that
he's got *nothing* in his hand anymore. He's just managed to hit an
absolute mine of combat, and he's got no intercept anymore, other than a
Sport Bike and maybe a London Evening Star, but the political deck has
been looking to steal that *anyway*. But maybe if I go back and look at
the stealth and bleed deck, he's actually got nothing in his hand
either. He had a wodge of combat defence and votes in his deck, just to
upset the apple cart a little and throw people off scent off the other
70 stealth and bleed cards in his deck, and they've all come at once.

At this point, as a judge, I have to balance what the players know with
what they can be reasonably be expected to believe. It might just
happen that the shuffles have gone so that player A should be able to
destroy player B. But I can't *tell* them that, and if I were to break
up a deal based on the empirical evidence, rather than what the players
could be reasonably expected to believe, I *will* tell them something.
Probably "Umm, something's odd here." If you look at your stealth bleed
hand and are being told "No, you can't make that deal with the
intercept/bounce deck", it doesn't take a genius to work out that
something may well be up with that deck.

In the context of clever play: Is a player just bullshitting me in order
to maximise their final chances? Are they just *saying* all that so
that they can knock out someone else from the running by giving other
people extra VPs? And are they, per my warnings above, just someone who
is much, much better with creative explanations than me? Or other
people?

On top of that, there's real life. Are they just a bad player? I can't
easily intervene in play just because someone's a novice and that's not
the best deal they could make. Maybe they don't know what cards he's
got, or how his deck's likely to perform, but I do. I still can't
intervene.

Added on top of this would be the fact that you have to tell players who
are trying to get table wins and VPs using solely in game methods, "No,
you can't." (I note "in game methods" to distinguish this from "out of
game methods", e.g. bribery, collusion.) You now have players playing
with contradictory statements. "You must maximise your VPs or Table
Wins." "You cannot do that using VP splitting deals." And with a judge
having to look over several tables, deciding when a player is
legitimately trying to make a long-term but without a guarantee of
splitting deal and when a player is trying to make what *seems* like a
long-term but without a guarantee of splitting deal, even though
everyone on the table fully understands what is *really* meant, it may
not be entirely practical to have a full understanding of the situation.

>is better to keep-on allowing a lot of Vps-Based-deals,
>but legally allowing to a table-win-player to "give away"
>the remaining Vps by potential (un-sanctionable at that point) collusion
>OR
> is better to disallow at all such "giving away" Vps,
>but minimizing the chanches of Vps-based-delas?

If you disallow VP splitting deals, they will still happen. They will
simply happen with the players who are quick-witted and gifted verbally.

I don't see that as a desirable outcome.

>> What would you do with all the legitimate deals you've just torn up?
>
>good question.
>We should see if those kind deals are fundamental for the game,
>and,above all, for the tournament enviroment (for which i raised
>the point).

The fundamental problem is that people are people and play to win, in
many instances. (Allowing playing for fun to be kept separate for now,
in the context of highly competitive tournament environments - where
these questions matter.)

How confident are you that you can spot the difference between a covert
VP splitting deal and long-term non-VP splitting mutual-co-operation?

How confident are you that, when people are playing in non-native
languages, they can reasonably be expected to understand the difference?

How confident are you that players who are motivated and competitive
won't play to the very edge of legal behaviour, taking advantage of the
loop-holes other players miss?

How confident are you that things won't go unvoiced, unspoken or
otherwise understood? If two people from the same regular play-group
sit at the same table, how confident are you that they don't already
know each other's play-styles well enough that - collusion/bribery apart
- they can't already make VP splitting deals, understanding what the
other person means, without it being properly noticed by others?

Collusion in and of itself is rarely that big an issue *anyway*. It
tends to come up most in arguments for things like the continental
championships, in situations where two people from the same country help
each other out.

If two players can demonstrate in game reasons and in game benefits for
a deal, and they're both maximising their VPs and table wins (as
appropriate), then they *may* be colluding, yes. (This is not, in and
of itself, a necessity.) But they also have to generate a scenario
where such co-operation is a possibility. They have to be on the same
table (in a 30 player tournament, that may well happen, yes) and they
have to be in a scenario where it's to their benefit. That doesn't just
happen, because they can't guarantee anything. One may be next to the
other (perfectly possible) at which point, if no offensive action is
taken at all, a player could easily call a judge over.

As LSJ stated, "Mercy on your prey for no reason is clearly not in your
interest. Your object when you sit down is to oust your prey - why the
sudden wave of mercy when you've finally achieved that goal?" [LSJ
20010120]

Side note: There are, of course, the other ways in which
collusion can be detected - the physical handing over of bribes.
But we can assume that the players engaging in such are not
going to do those.

When players are not playing to maximise their chances (never bleeding,
never taking offensive action, for certain values of "never") a judge
can intervene. For instance:

"Disrupting the table dynamic *is* severely disruptive.
Throwing a game (losing on purpose) is disruptive."
(Also [LSJ 20010120])

Similarly, again the same post, re: play in your best interest:

"Always. Or at least - in your perceived best interests (since
none of the players has perfect knowledge of the other players'
hands, decks, and intentions)."

It's worth bearing in mind that the term "disruptive" is the term used
in Unsportsman Like conduct. (A term referenced in that post.)

With collusion, therefore, first of all it's hard to generate *anyway*.
In any large tournament (where large is about a dozen-15 players),
you'll not see the same person again. Much larger than that, you may
not even see a given person anyway.

(Though, as lessons that probability sucks, I do seem to have a knack
for randomly allocating people who've travelled a long way onto the same
table. e.g. the Durings.)

So it may not even have a chance to occur and when it can, you can often
intervene on more obvious grounds *anyway*.

Whereas VP split deals occur regularly. If we take the suggestion that
any deal that results in a reasonable chance of securing VPs is banned,

"Again, if a deal is made were the probable outcome is a VP-
split, then it should be treated as a VP-splitting deal."

This is what we're being asked to ban. And any deal that goes something
like "Give me a little help, he's being monstrous to me, can you rush
Arika and I'll help you pass that vote?" certainly stands a good chance
of helping them get some VPs each, with cross-table interaction.

So now, even when we don't think they're colluding (a judgement call,
and one I exercise very lightly anyway) and we do think the deal is in
their best interests, we have to decide not only if they're *trying* to
split VPs, but also if "the probable outcome is a VP-split". Any
significant deal is going to stand a good chance of falling under that.

And that's not going to have judges making ad-hoc, inconsistent
decisions every five minutes and prevent people from playing to maximise
their TW and VPs. Definitely not.

along with deals with you. This (PDG) is the 'game' popular with

didn't care that there was a VP split going to happen eventually. They

two points:

make any deals, since causing the loss of the Game Win is, in the long
run, almost as important for the losing players as eeking out whatever
small VPs they're going to get in the game.

are built-in as part of the game, you have alliances, which people don't
like when they're not on the "winning" side.

as simplistic and unreasonable. You cannot say that every game of VTES
is a "goat" game because in the end, VTES is just that, a GAME, the
stakes are not life and death, and the measure of how ANY player
plays, whether cut-throat or diplomat, is representative of what that
player finds entertaining and enjoyable. To wish for every game to be
the vicious, every-man-for-himself goat's game is a personal wish, the
goat's game is what you yourself find entertaining. But given the
spectrum of personalities in game players, you cannot reasonably
expect all others to share your view, at least not if you expect some
of them to enjoy the game.

Perhaps a more realistic description of the two types of players in
VTES is that of FINITE players and INFINITE players (ala James Carse,
to give credit). FINITE players only play to win and in the pursuit of
this desire tend to forget (as is the requirement of ALL finite play)
that the game is just a game. The atmosphere at a table of finite
players is tense, cut-throat, and highly fierce and competitive. I
openly acknowledge that this type of play can be entertaining, but I
speculate that not every player would share this view. There are
external factors to EVERY game, things going on in a player's life
outside of the game that he may be unwittingly bringing with him to
the VTES table. Be disgusted with it all you wish, but to a certain
extent some element of humanity is inevitable in all games. Given
this, playing against "sheep" is going to happen, regularly, and
indeed people who were goats last week, may realistically be sheep the
next, and vice versa.

Furthermore, finite players tend to insist that everyone play within
the same explicit boundries they are playing within, using the same
interpretation of the game, since indeed it allows the definition of
victory to be reached more clearly. That's fine, I mean, we all need
to agree on the rules before we begin or the game unravels. It stops
being a game though when you begin forcing your view of the game on
others. A game definition that is forced upon other players (rather
than freely agreed upon by all players) is not a game.

Comparatively, Infinite players play finite games (like VTES)
primarily to enjoy the act of playing, victory is pursued, but can be
coincidental since the primary goal is to just have fun (and we can
agree that we all have different definitions of what we find fun,
yes?) so things like cross-table diplomacy, alliance making, are
entertained to expand upon the finite rules and boundries of the game.
Indeed you mention this yourself--the diplomatic metagame is not
covered in the VTES rulebook. This is not so that it can be eliminated
as an element of VTES, but because such an element can never be
defined by rules, since doing so would undermine it's very nature.
Finite players play within the boundries of the game, infinite players
play WITH the boundries themselves.

It's important to emphasize that infinite players still play finite
games, it's just that their attitude toward such games differs from
people who are primarily finite players. Finite players tend to act
competitively. Infinite players act playfully.

My point is, lighten up, dude: approach the game from a more playful,
less cut-throat standpoint, put yourself in the shoes of someone who
is just there to enjoy themselves and realize that not everyone enjoys
what you enjoy.

-Matt
